subject: political-science
readings: Ashbee & Hurst (2020), 'The Trump foreign policy record and the concept of transformational change,' Global Affairs 6(1): 5 to 19 · Putnam (1988), 'Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two Level Games,' International Organization 42(3): 427 to 460 (to p.435)

cards.front: What is the **"black box"** in IR theory?
cards.back: It treats a state's internal politics as unopened: inputs (the international system) go in, policy comes out, with nothing examined between.
cards.hint: System in, policy out, nothing examined between.

cards.front: What does **opening the black box** mean in this lecture?
cards.back: Examining the **domestic** processes inside a state, showing foreign policy is shaped by domestic and international variables that **interact**.
cards.hint: Look inside the state, not just the system.

cards.front: Which theory keeps the state **black boxed** because only anarchy and power matter?
cards.back: **Structural realism (Waltz).** Regime type barely matters; what counts is anarchy, relative capabilities, and the survival imperative.
cards.hint: Anarchy · survival · Waltz.

cards.front: According to structural realism, why must any state prioritise its own security?
cards.back: Because international relations are **anarchic** and trust is limited, so every state (democracy or autocracy) must ensure its own survival.
cards.hint: Anarchy leaves survival to each state.

cards.front: Which theory cares about a state's regime character but still won't open domestic processes?
cards.back: **Liberal internationalism (Ikenberry).** It looks at the character of political systems but still doesn't examine internal processes closely.
cards.hint: Interdependence · IOs · Ikenberry.

cards.front: What is the **"Golden Arches"** theory of peace?
cards.back: A tongue in cheek liberal claim that no two countries with **McDonald's** have gone to war, a stand in for trade **interdependence** deterring conflict.
cards.hint: No two countries with McDonald's fight.

cards.front: Name the approach: the study of foreign policy as a product of domestic processes **and** international structure.
cards.back: **Foreign Policy Analysis (FPA).**
cards.hint: Three letters; opens the black box.

cards.front: How does **neoclassical realism** turn the same systemic pressure into different policies?
cards.back: 1) **Systemic start**: relative power and anarchy pressure every state. 2) **Domestic filter**: pressures pass through intervening variables (leaders' perceptions, state society relations, institutions). 3) **Divergent output**: the same pressure yields different policies across states.
cards.hint: Structure pushes → domestic filter → different outputs.

cards.front: Name the bridge theory: keeps realism's systemic start but filters pressure through domestic variables.
cards.back: **Neoclassical realism.**
cards.hint: Structure pushes, domestic politics filters.

cards.front: What are the **five families of domestic variable** that shape foreign policy?
cards.back: 1) **Individuals / core actors** (leaders). 2) **Ideas & ideologies** (the guiding paradigm). 3) **Bureaucratic cultures** (agencies, factions). 4) **Interest groups & constituencies** (lobbying). 5) **Public opinion** (mass attitudes, note salience).
cards.hint: People · ideas · bureaucracies · interests · publics.

cards.front: Who wrote *"the history of the world is but the biography of great men"*?
cards.back: **Carlyle (1840)**, giving the **"great man theory of history"** (the individuals / core actors variable).
cards.hint: Leaders as history's engine.

cards.front: What is the blind spot of the **great man theory**?
cards.back: Focusing on individuals **neglects structural forces**: an individual only focus **underestimates context**.
cards.hint: Leaders alone miss the structure.

cards.front: In the interest groups variable, how does **instrumental power** differ from **structural power**?
cards.back: **Instrumental power**: direct lobbying, campaigning, contributions, the **"revolving door."** **Structural power**: business's leverage from its control over investment and jobs, working even without lobbying. One is what business **does**, the other what business **is**.
cards.hint: What business does vs what business is.

cards.front: What is **salience** in public opinion?
cards.back: How much the public actually **attends to** an issue. For foreign policy it is usually **low** except in acute crisis or heavy losses (Durant & Diehl 1989).
cards.hint: How much the public is even paying attention.

cards.front: What does the **Vietnam** case show about public opinion?
cards.back: Disengagement was blamed on the war's growing unpopularity, but **salience** means opinion bites mainly under **heavy losses**. So public opinion is a real but **conditional** constraint.
cards.hint: Opinion bites mainly under heavy losses.

cards.front: Beyond Trump himself, what **enabled** his style to drive US foreign policy?
cards.back: The **relative weakness of checks and balances** in the foreign policy arena, plus deeper trends: **party polarisation**, **party homogenisation**, and a **populist shift**. An individual only story underestimates this context.
cards.hint: Weak checks + polarisation + homogenisation + populism.

cards.front: How did **Truman (1945 to 53)** lead the US into engagement, per the deck?
cards.back: Through several variables interacting at once: **individual** commitment, shifts in **economic elites**, and **strategic** pressure from the USSR.
cards.hint: Several variables at once.

cards.front: How does **Liberal Internationalism** differ from **militant / conservative internationalism (primacism)**?
cards.back: **LI**: post war open ended engagement and global leadership, building the UN, IMF, World Bank, GATT, NATO. **Primacism** (mainly Republicans, from the 1970s split): rejects LI's cooperative side and seeks US primacy via unilateral hard power, but keeps a moral purpose (democracy promotion, regime change).
cards.hint: Cooperative liberal order vs unilateral primacy (still moralistic).

cards.front: Name the concept: US primacy as the organising aim, hard power used unilaterally, sidelining multilateralism.
cards.back: **Primacism.**
cards.hint: Primacy as the whole point.

cards.front: Which institutions did **Liberal Internationalism** build after WWII?
cards.back: Internationally the **UN, IMF, World Bank, GATT, NATO**, and at home a **national security state** (National Security Act 1947: DoD, Joint Chiefs, NSC, CIA).
cards.hint: Global bodies plus a national security state.

cards.front: What are the five propositions of Trump's **populist nationalist paradigm** (Ashbee & Hurst)?
cards.back: 1) **The nation is core** (ethnicity/culture, not ideals). 2) **Zero sum competition** for hegemony. 3) **Anti globalism** and global elites. 4) **Trade subordinated to the nation** (bilateral, not multilateral). 5) **Moral vision abandoned** (no regime change or democracy promotion).
cards.hint: Nation · zero sum · anti globalism · bilateral trade · no moral vision.

cards.front: In the reading's formula, what is Trump's paradigm equal to?
cards.back: **Primacism + economic nationalism + "principled realism"** = conservative internationalism **minus the moral purpose**. He keeps unilateral hard power but drops democracy promotion and regime change.
cards.hint: Conservative internationalism minus the moral crusade.

cards.front: What is **transformational change** (Ashbee & Hurst)?
cards.back: A **lasting** shift across **four linked elements** (paradigm, interests, institutions, logics), not merely dramatic but passing change.
cards.hint: Must last, across four elements.

cards.front: What must shift in each of the **four elements** of transformational change?
cards.back: 1) **Paradigm**: ideas/goals/instruments become **"common sense"** (Hall). 2) **Interests**: new interests and **coalitions** grip power (Skowronek). 3) **Institutions**: formal and informal **reordering**. 4) **Logics**: new enduring **chains of events / incentives** (path dependence).
cards.hint: Paradigm · interests · institutions · logics.

cards.front: Why is the **1940s Liberal Internationalism** shift the model of a completed transformation?
cards.back: All four elements shifted **and stuck**: paradigm (global leadership), interests (New Deal plus Wall Street coalition sideline isolationists), institutions (UN/IMF/NATO plus national security state), logics (enduring collective security). It is the yardstick for judging Trump.
cards.hint: All four shifted and endured.

cards.front: What is the verdict when the four element framework is run on **Trump (2017+)**?
cards.back: The **beginnings** of transformation, but **"incipient, partial and variegated"**: ideational shift strongest; institutional and interest shifts incomplete (core alliances intact); logics hardest to read this early.
cards.hint: Incipient, partial and variegated.

cards.front: What is **embeddedness** in Ashbee & Hurst?
cards.back: Ideas become a lasting transformation only when **rooted in supportive interests and institutions**, so they outlive the leader.
cards.hint: Ideas need roots in interests + institutions.

cards.front: Why was Trump's first term only **"proto transformational"**?
cards.back: His primacism was pursued inconsistently and **weakly embedded**: he **marginalised** the national security bureaucracy but did **not rebuild** it into a self sustaining machine for the new paradigm.
cards.hint: Ideas never got rooted in interests and institutions.

cards.front: Name the concept: populism is a **"crust"** laid over other ideologies (Mudde).
cards.back: A **"thin" ideology.**
cards.hint: A thin crust on thicker ideologies.

cards.front: What two reasons does the reading give that Trump's change may **not stick**?
cards.back: 1) Populism is a **thin ideology** (a crust), so the administration could be pulled **back** toward conservative internationalism. 2) The US stays **locked into** its key post war security institutions.
cards.hint: Thin ideology + locked into institutions.

cards.front: How is a negotiation **one game played at two levels** in Putnam's model?
cards.back: One game, two levels: **Level I** = bargaining between negotiators at the international table. **Level II** = domestic discussions about whether to **ratify** the deal. The leader sits at **both boards at once**, joined by the **win set**.
cards.hint: One player, two boards, joined by win sets.

cards.front: What is the **win set** in Putnam's model?
cards.back: The set of all Level I deals that would win **ratification** at Level II.
cards.hint: The deals your home side would ratify.

cards.front: In Putnam, when is an international deal possible?
cards.back: Only where the two **win sets overlap**. Bigger win sets make agreement more likely, but risk a deal your public dislikes.
cards.hint: Where the two win sets overlap.

cards.front: Name the idea: being **tied down at home** is a bargaining asset abroad.
cards.back: The **Schelling conjecture**: a **smaller win set** can give a negotiator **more** bargaining power.
cards.hint: Tied hands as a bargaining chip.

cards.front: In Putnam, how does **voluntary defection** differ from **involuntary defection**?
cards.back: **Voluntary defection**: a rational leader **reneges** by choice. **Involuntary defection**: the leader **can't deliver** because **ratification fails at home**. It shows domestic and international politics are entangled, not separate.
cards.hint: Won't deliver vs can't deliver.

cards.front: Along which **four dimensions** does the domestic vs international balance vary systematically?
cards.back: 1) **Time period**: domestic variables matter less in acute crisis. 2) **State size**: small states have fewer options. 3) **Regime type**: liberal democracies are more exposed to domestic pressure. 4) **Policy arena**: some issues, especially **trade**, draw more domestic engagement.
cards.hint: Time/crisis · size · regime · arena (esp. trade).

cards.front: What single **red thread** question should you ask of any foreign policy episode?
cards.back: Which **domestic variables** are in play, how do they **interact** with the international situation, and is the change **transformational** or just a passing shift?
cards.hint: Theory sets the stage; home decides the play.
